name: Battle of Raphia
info: Ptolemy IV of Egypt defeated Antiochus III of the Seleucid Empire near Raphia on 22 June 217 BCE, in the Fourth Syrian War, and kept Coele-Syria for Egypt until Antiochus took it back at Panium in 200 BCE.

facts.place: Near the small town of Rafah (Raphia) in Syria, on the coast road between Egypt and Gaza, in the region of Coele-Syria; modern Rafah
facts.sides: Ptolemaic Egypt under Ptolemy IV Philopator; the Seleucid Empire under Antiochus III the Great. According to Polybius, Ptolemy had 70,000 infantry, 5,000 cavalry and 73 elephants, and Antiochus 62,000 infantry, 6,000 cavalry and 102 elephants
facts.outcome: The Ptolemaic army drove the Seleucid army from the field, and Antiochus asked for a truce to bury his dead. Ptolemy's victory secured Coele-Syria for Egypt.

t: It is the only known battle in which African and Asian elephants were used against each other, and Polybius says the larger Indian elephants easily routed the Africans.
Antiochus routed the Ptolemaic horse facing him and rode off in pursuit, but the Ptolemaic phalanxes drove back the Seleucid phalanxes in his absence and his army broke before he returned.

The large native Egyptian phalanx that helped win the battle is said to have given the Egyptians a new self-confidence, which Polybius counted among the causes of the secession of Upper Egypt from 207.
dyk: Antiochus III's army included 102 Indian war elephants against Ptolemy IV's 73 African ones, the only known battle in which the two kinds met.
ev: The Fourth Syrian War begins between Ptolemaic Egypt under Ptolemy IV and the Seleucid Empire under Antiochus III
Both armies are on campaign through Syria and meet near the town of Rafah
Theodotus the Aetolian enters the Ptolemaic camp to kill Ptolemy but finds the king's tent empty
After five days of skirmishing the two armies are drawn up and the battle is fought
Priests meet at Memphis to give thanks for the victory, and a stele honours Ptolemy as pharaoh in Greek as well as Egyptian
Upper Egypt secedes under the pharaohs Hugronaphor and Ankhmakis, a separate kingdom lasting nearly twenty years
Antiochus defeats the army of Ptolemy V Epiphanes at Panium and recaptures Coele-Syria and Judea

sections.background:
Ptolemaic Egypt and the Seleucid Empire were the two largest Hellenistic kingdoms of the 3rd century BCE, and they repeatedly fought for control of Syria in a series of conflicts known as the Syrian Wars. The Fourth Syrian War began in 219 BCE. Egypt was then ruled by Ptolemy IV, who was king and pharaoh, and the Seleucid Empire by Antiochus III the Great.

The prize was Coele-Syria. Theodotus of Aetolia, who had served Ptolemy, betrayed him and handed much of Coele-Syria and Phoenicia over to Antiochus, and he afterwards commanded the Silver Shields in Antiochus's army. By 217 BCE both armies were on campaign through Syria, and they met near the small Syrian town of Rafah.

Antiochus first set up his camp at a distance of 10 stadia, about 2 kilometres, from his adversary's, and then moved to only 5 stadia, about 1 kilometre. The fighting began with a series of small skirmishes around the edge of each army. One night Theodotus, the former officer of Ptolemy, slipped into the Ptolemaic camp and made for what he took to be the king's tent in order to assassinate him. Ptolemy was not there, and the plot failed.
sections.forces:
The Seleucid army, according to the figures given for its contingents, was made up of 5,000 lightly armed Dahae, Carmanians and Cilicians under Byttacus the Macedonian, 10,000 phalangites, the Argyraspides or Silver Shields, under Theodotus of Aetolia, and 20,000 Macedonian phalangites under Nicarchus and Theodotus Hemiolius. There were also 5,000 Medes, Cissians, Cadusii and Carmanians, 10,000 Arabians under Zabdibelus, 5,000 Greek mercenaries under Hippolochus the Thessalian, and Cretans and Neocretans. Antiochus had 4,000 horsemen under his nephew Antipater and 2,000 under Themison, and 102 Indian war elephants under Philip and Myischos.

Ptolemy had just ended a major recruitment and retraining plan with the help of many mercenary generals. His force included 3,000 hypaspists, the Agema, 2,000 peltasts, 25,000 Macedonian phalangites, 8,000 Greek mercenaries, Cretan and Neocretan archers, 3,000 Libyans, and 20,000 Egyptians under his chief minister Sosibius, trained in the Macedonian way to fight alongside the Macedonians. His Household Cavalry numbered 700, and the local and Libyan horse another 2,300. He had 73 elephants of African stock.

According to Polybius, Ptolemy had 70,000 infantry, 5,000 cavalry and 73 war elephants, and Antiochus 62,000 infantry, 6,000 cavalry and 102 elephants.
sections.course:
After five days of skirmishing, the two kings decided to array their troops for battle. Both placed their phalangites in the centre. Next to them they put the lightly armed troops and the mercenaries, in front of which stood the elephants, and further out on the wings the cavalry. The kings spoke to their soldiers and took their places, Ptolemy on his left and Antiochus on his right wing.

At the start the elephants on the wings of both armies charged. Ptolemy's smaller African elephants retreated in panic before the larger Indian ones and ran back through the friendly infantry behind them, causing disorder. Antiochus led his cavalry to the right and rode past the left wing of the Ptolemaic elephants to charge the enemy horse. The two phalanxes then engaged in a stiff and chaotic fight. Antiochus had the Silver Shields, while Ptolemy's Macedonians were strengthened by the Egyptian phalanx. The right wing of Ptolemy was retreating and wheeling to protect itself from the panicked elephants, and Ptolemy rode to the centre to urge his phalanx on. On the far right of the Ptolemaic line, his cavalry was routing its opponents.

Antiochus routed the Ptolemaic horse facing him and pursued the fleeing enemy in a mass, believing he had won the day. The Ptolemaic phalanxes in the meantime drove the Seleucid phalanxes back. When Antiochus rode back his troops were routed and could no longer be regrouped.
sections.aftermath:
After the battle Antiochus wanted to regroup and make camp outside Raphia, but most of his men had already found refuge inside the town, and he was forced to enter it himself. He then marched to Gaza and asked Ptolemy for the customary truce to bury the dead, which was granted.

According to Polybius, the Seleucids lost a little under 10,000 infantry, about 300 horse and 5 elephants, and 4,000 men were taken prisoner. The Ptolemaic losses were 1,500 infantry, 700 horse and 16 elephants. Most of the Ptolemies' elephants were captured by the Seleucids.

Ptolemy's victory secured the province of Coele-Syria for Egypt, but it was only a respite. At the Battle of Panium in 200 BCE Antiochus defeated the army of Ptolemy's young son, Ptolemy V Epiphanes, and recaptured Coele-Syria and Judea.
sections.sources:
The figures for the two armies and for the losses are those of Polybius, and the descriptions of the elephants and of the king's speeches to his troops also come from him. The elephants have been a subject of study. Polybius describes the Asian elephants of Antiochus, brought from India, as larger and stronger than Ptolemy's African ones, and it was once theorised that these were African forest elephants. Recent DNA research has suggested instead that they were African bush elephants, culled from a population of smaller animals still found in Eritrea, and another possibility is the now extinct North African elephant, about 2.4 metres high at the shoulder.

The stele that records the convocation of priests at Memphis in November 217, held to give thanks for the victory, survives, inscribed in Greek and in hieroglyphic and demotic Egyptian. Some biblical commentators see the battle as the one referred to in Daniel 11:11.
sections.legacy:
The battle was one of the largest of the Hellenistic kingdoms and of the ancient world, and it determined the sovereignty of Coele-Syria, although only until 200 BCE. Ptolemy owed his victory in part to a properly equipped and trained native Egyptian phalanx, which for the first time formed a large proportion of his phalangites and ended his manpower problems.

The self-confidence the Egyptians gained was credited by Polybius as one of the causes of the secession of Upper Egypt in 207 to 186 BCE under the pharaohs Hugronaphor and Ankhmakis, who created a separate kingdom that lasted nearly twenty years. The battle marks a turning point in Ptolemaic history. The native Egyptian element in the administration and culture of the 2nd century BCE grew in influence, driven in part by the major role Egyptians had played in the battle and in part by the financial pressures on the state, made worse by the cost of the war itself.

The Memphis stele gives Ptolemy full pharaonic honours in the Greek texts as well as the Egyptian ones for the first time, and this later became the norm.

summary: At Raphia on 22 June 217 BCE the army of Ptolemy IV of Egypt defeated that of Antiochus III of the Seleucid Empire, in a battle where African and Asian elephants met. Egypt kept Coele-Syria, and the large native Egyptian phalanx changed its politics.
notes: The article is thin on the course; the sections' length is made up from the article's own facts, and the sources section is short because the article names only Polybius and the Memphis stele.

The article says Ptolemy's cavalry 'on the Ptolemaic far right' routed its opponents, while also placing Ptolemy on his left; the wing positions are as the article gives them and are not fully clear. It says Antiochus rode 'to the right' past the left wing of the Ptolemaic elephants.
The article gives only Polybius's totals; its contingent figures (Seleucid and Ptolemaic) are listed in part only, with Thracians, Gauls and some others left out for length.

Left out as plainly garbled or doubtful: 'under the Aspasianus the Mede'; Eurylochus is named as commander of both a Seleucid Cretan and a Ptolemaic hypaspist contingent (two men, one name, as the article has it).
The article's date is 22 June 217 BC; no dispute is stated.
The elephant sentence in the article, 'Regardless of origin, according to Polybius ... could not bear the smell, sound, and sight', is rendered as Polybius's view in the takeaway.
